content: The Italian Plague of 1629–1631 was a series of outbreaks of bubonic plague that occurred in northern Italy between 1629 and 1631. This epidemic, often referred to as the Great Plague of Milan, resulted in the deaths of approximately 280,000 people, with the cities of Lombardy experiencing particularly high mortality rates. It is considered one of the final outbreaks of the centuries-long pandemic of bubonic plague that began with the Black Death. The plague was introduced to the city of Mantua in 1629 by German and French troops, who carried the disease as a consequence of troop movements associated with the Thirty Years' War (1618–1648). Venetian troops, who had also been infected, retreated into northern and central Italy, further spreading the infection. By October 1629, the plague had reached Milan, the major commercial hub of Lombardy. Despite the implementation of effective public health measures, such as quarantine and restrictions on the entry of German soldiers and trade goods, the disease persisted in the city. A significant outbreak occurred in March 1630, largely due to the relaxation of health measures during the carnival season. This was followed by a second wave of infections in the spring and summer of 1631. Milan ultimately suffered approximately 60,000 fatalities out of a total population of 130,000. To the east of Lombardy, the Republic of Venice was also affected by the plague in 1630–1631. The city of Venice itself was severely impacted, with recorded deaths of 46,000 people out of a population of 140,000. Some historians argue that the drastic loss of life and its subsequent impact on commerce contributed to the decline of Venice as a major commercial and political power. The papal city of Bologna experienced an estimated 15,000 deaths due to the plague, while neighboring smaller cities such as Modena and Parma were also heavily affected. The outbreak extended northward into Tyrol, an alpine region spanning western Austria and northern Italy. Later outbreaks of bubonic plague in Italy included the city of Florence between 1630 and 1633, as well as the areas surrounding Naples, Rome, and Genoa in 1656–1657. The 1630 plague in Milan serves as the backdrop for several chapters of Alessandro Manzoni's novel The Betrothed (I promessi sposi). Although a work of fiction, Manzoni's depiction of the conditions and events in plague-stricken Milan is historically accurate and extensively documented through primary sources that he researched. A section of the book, which was later removed, described the historical trial and execution of three individuals accused of being plague-spreaders. This account was subsequently published in a separate booklet titled Storia della colonna infame (History of the Infamous Pillar).
